title: Mandavya and the measured rod
hookLine: a silent sage is punished as a thief, and calls even Dharma to account
carry: a just rod is a measured rod
tomorrow: crowned at last. who does a new king still have to listen to?

lines: A SAGE KEEPS A VOW OF SILENCE.
cards: A sage named Mandavya sits outside his hermitage under a vow of silence. Thieves fleeing the king's guards hide their loot there. The guards find it and ask him where the thieves went.
He says nothing; he's keeping his vow. So the king, without another question, has him punished with the thieves, on a stake. The thieves die.
Mandavya doesn't. The king hears, rushes out, begs forgiveness, and tries to pull the stake free. He can't.
Its tip stays in the sage's body, and from then on people call him Ani-Mandavya, Mandavya of the spike.

teach.h: EVEN DHARMA IS CALLED TO ACCOUNT.
teach.b: Then Mandavya goes to Dharma himself, the lord of justice, and asks what he did to deserve it. As a child, Dharma says, you pierced a little insect with a blade of grass. A punishment that size, for that?
Mandavya sets a new rule, that nothing done before fourteen counts as sin, and curses Dharma to be born a man; in the Mahabharata he comes back as Vidura, the wise counselor.
Even the lord of justice answers for a rod out of measure. The Arthashastra, this week's handbook on power, makes the same demand. It sets out three rulers.

teach.h: TOO HARD: FEARED. TOO MILD: DESPISED.
teach.b: One strikes too hard, and people are terrified. One is too mild, and people despise him.

One uses the rod justly, after thinking it through, and he is honored. Used out of desire, anger or ignorance, it says, the rod enrages even hermits in the forest. It's hard not to hear Mandavya there.
Our Buddhist neighbors look at the same rod from where it lands.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death." The Pali word is danda, the same rod. Both weigh it by the one who feels it.

teach.h: A JUST ROD IS A MEASURED ROD.
teach.b: The difference: the Arthashastra keeps the rod in a just hand; the verse asks each person not to strike.

how: The Mahabharata tells Mandavya's story as the reason Vidura, Dharma born as a man, came into the world; teachers of the Arthashastra point to its passage on the rod's measure, and Buddhists know Dhammapada 129–130 as a teaching on not harming.

an old ruling book's rule: the harshest king is the safest
an old ruling book's rule: power, measured to the deed

games.q: the sage, the rod and a verse — tap the pairs.
p: a silent sage punished as a thief

s: Mandavya was punished because he helped the thieves
he was keeping a vow of silence; the king struck without asking another question.
the Dhammapada's word for punishment there is danda, the rod
the same word: one text weighs the king's rod, the other the fear of the one it falls on.
Buddhist and Hindu texts say the very same thing about the rod
both weigh it by the one who feels it; the Arthashastra keeps it in a just hand, the verse asks each person not to strike.

games.q: you're babysitting two kids, and one hits the other over a toy. by the measured rod, what's the consequence?
o: no screens for a week, so it never happens again.
a short break and a quick talk, then back to playing.
laugh it off. kids hit; nobody needs a consequence.
games.why: too harsh breeds fear, too mild gets ignored. a just consequence, thought through, fits the deed. even Dharma had to answer for a punishment bigger than the wrong.

practice: Notice your hands and your jaw. If they're gripping, let them soften; if they've gone slack, gather them to a gentle hold. Rest in that middle grip.
If you pray, ask quietly for a fair mind before you judge anyone today.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: danda, the rod, measured. Not too harsh, not too mild, and thought through.

orig.note: Sanskrit danda, a rod or staff; the Pali daṇḍa in Dhammapada 129 is the same word.

carryVoice: Keep this: a just rod is a measured rod. Even Dharma answered to Mandavya. Until tomorrow.
